q: Which grape is grown for Lazio's red DOCG, in the hills southeast of Rome toward Frosinone?
exp: Cesanese gives a perfumed, medium-bodied red with a faintly bitter finish, and the Piglio zone is its stronghold. Lazio's other DOCGs are both white and both at Frascati.

q: Much of what reaches the bottle as Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is not Trebbiano Toscano. Which variety is often there instead?
exp: The denomination permits Bombino Bianco as well as the distinct local Trebbiano Abruzzese, and the two have been confused in the vineyard for generations. The rare wines with real depth come from the local variety, not from Trebbiano Toscano.

q: Teramo's hills in the north of Abruzzo carry the region's own DOCG for Montepulciano. What is it called?
exp: Higher, cooler sites under the Gran Sasso give a firmer wine than the coastal plain does, and the ageing requirement is longer. The bulk of the region's Montepulciano is bottled at DOC level below it.

q: A once nearly extinct Abruzzo white, now widely planted, shares its name with a sheep's cheese. Name the grape.
exp: It was down to a handful of vines by the 1980s and is now the region's most fashionable white. Small berries and thick skins give it more weight and alcohol than Trebbiano.

q: Molise's native red variety was nearly lost and now carries a DOC of its own. Name it.
exp: The name comes from a dialect word for dye, which describes the colour it gives. It grows best high inland, where Molise's hills climb toward the Apennine spine.

q: Aglianico ripens so late in Irpinia that picking often runs into which month?
exp: It is among the last varieties harvested anywhere in Italy, and the long hang keeps acidity high while tannin slowly resolves. That combination is why Taurasi is built to age.

q: Vines at Campi Flegrei grow in deep volcanic sand and many still stand on their own roots. What does that sand keep out?
opts: Phylloxera, which cannot live in it
Downy mildew, which cannot spread in it
Spring frost, which cannot settle on it
Botrytis, which cannot take hold in it
exp: The louse cannot travel through loose siliceous sand to reach a root, so ungrafted vines survive there. Sardinia's Sulcis and Colares in Portugal depend on the same accident of soil.

q: Which pair of grapes makes the white and the red of Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio?
exp: Coda di Volpe means fox's tail and describes the shape of the bunch. Both grapes are grown on the volcano's ash and lava soils inside the national park.

q: The village that gives Greco di Tufo its name was long mined for a mineral used in the cellar. Which mineral?
exp: The mines closed decades ago but the smoky, struck-match note in the wine is still routinely traced to them. Sulphur remains the winemaker's principal antioxidant and antiseptic.

q: Which Campanian white takes on hazelnut and honey with age and is grown in the hills east of Naples?
exp: Fiano is low-yielding and thick-skinned, and unusually for a southern white it improves for years in bottle. Altitude around Avellino supplies the acidity that makes the ageing possible.

q: Campania's second red is nicknamed dove's foot for the colour of its stalks at harvest. Name the grape.
exp: The stems turn red as the fruit ripens, which is what the dialect name records. It gives a softer, earlier-drinking wine than Aglianico and is often blended in to lighten it.

q: Vines on the Amalfi coast are worked on narrow terraces held by dry stone walls. Which DOC covers them?
exp: Furore, Ravello and Tramonti are its named subzones, all of them tended by hand because no machine can reach the terraces. Some Tramonti vines are ungrafted and well over a century old.

q: Head-trained bush vines stand free of wires across much of the Salento. What is that training system called in Italian?
exp: The vine forms its own low goblet, shading the fruit and needing no trellis in a dry, windy place. Yields are small and every operation has to be done by hand.

q: Castel del Monte takes its name from a thirteenth-century castle in Puglia. Which native red is bottled there at DOCG level as a Riserva?
exp: Nero di Troia, also called Uva di Troia, ripens late and carries firm tannin, so it needs the extra ageing a Riserva demands. It is the third of Puglia's major reds after Primitivo and Negroamaro.

q: On the Ionian coast of Calabria, the Ciro zone builds its red on which grape?
exp: Gaglioppo gives a pale, savoury, high-alcohol red with more tannin than its colour suggests. Magliocco is the region's other serious native red, grown further west and south.

q: Puglia gained a DOCG for a naturally sweet style of Primitivo. Which town names it?
exp: The sweet version stops fermentation while sugar remains rather than adding spirit, which is what naturale records. The dry Primitivo di Manduria from the same town stays at DOC.
